tagline: An Army supply corridor links forts and a Civil War battlefield.
intro: The Frontier Military Historic Byway crosses eastern Kansas on a mix of state highways, US highways and Interstate 435, linking Leavenworth with the Oklahoma border. Kansas Tourism gives the historic byway’s length as 168 miles and highlights its forts and Civil War cavalry battlefield. At Fort Scott, the drive reaches the Osage Plains beside the Marmaton River. Leavenworth sits on the Missouri River’s west bank; farther south, Pittsburg occupies an Ozark Highlands landscape of prairie and forest.

The military road was built between 1838 and 1844 to carry soldiers and supplies among Fort Leavenworth, Fort Scott and Fort Gibson. Fort Scott was established on that road in 1842. After the Army abandoned the post in 1853, its buildings were auctioned to settlers; during the Civil War it became a headquarters, supply depot and training center.

Starting near Fort Leavenworth’s gates, follow K-7 south to K-5, then I-435 south and east to US 69. Farther south, Mine Creek Battlefield lies southwest of Pleasanton, followed by Fort Scott on US 69. US 69 Alternate reaches Baxter Springs on the Spring River before the byway ends at the Oklahoma line. Baxter Springs stands at the western edge of the Ozarks.

moments.title: Fort Leavenworth
moments.text: Colonel Henry Leavenworth and soldiers of the 3rd Infantry established this post in 1827 to protect the Santa Fe Trail. It later supplied the Army of the West during the Mexican–American War. The African-American 10th Cavalry Regiment formed here in 1866. A cavalry-rider statue honors the Buffalo Soldiers of the 9th and 10th Cavalry. Military education became another lasting role: the school William T. Sherman established in 1881 developed into the Army’s Command and General Staff College. The fort remains a United States Army installation within the city of Leavenworth, Kansas.

moments.title: Mine Creek Battlefield State Historic Site
moments.text: A wagon train stalled at a creek crossing made retreating Confederate troops vulnerable at Mine Creek. Sterling Price’s army had withdrawn into Kansas after its defeat at Westport on October 23, 1864. Two days later, Union cavalry under John F. Philips and Frederick W. Benteen caught up at the crossing and defeated the defenders. Confederate general John S. Marmaduke was among those captured. Preservation followed much later: Kansas legislators approved a 160-acre battlefield purchase in 1970, and a visitor center opened in 1998. Marked trails identify significant features of the battlefield for visitors.

moments.title: Fort Scott National Historic Site
moments.text: Fort Scott was built without defensive walls: open ground and available artillery made an enclosure unnecessary. Its soldiers instead built quarters and structures for animals and equipment along a 350-foot parade ground. Captain Thomas Swords, the quartermaster, struggled with shortages of skilled labor, timber and equipment. Officials halted further construction in 1850; the Army abandoned the post three years later in favor of Fort Riley farther west. The post later recruited and trained Black soldiers for the Union Army during the Civil War. The National Park Service preserves the structures, parade ground and tallgrass prairie as witnesses to the fort’s 1842–1873 history.
moments.notice: Notice the parade ground and restored tallgrass prairie at the historic site.
